items.author: Andrew Zinin
items.title: Beeswax and pine link crocodile mummies made centuries apart at one Egyptian site
items.summary: In a practice spanning centuries, ancient Egyptians mummified thousands of crocodiles they associated with Sobek, a god linked to the Nile, fertility and royal power. In one unique example, embalmers from the middle of the 1st millennium BC at Kom Ombo in southern Egypt mounted more than 25 hatchlings on reeds along the back and neck of a crocodile nearly 4 meters (13 feet) long. The arrangement may echo the way young crocodiles ride on their mother's back.

items.originalTitle: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.author: Will Steakin
items.title: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.summary: Ro Khanna hasn't launched a 2028 bid yet, but he already has a pioneer of the populist left in his corner. Progressive firebrand Cenk Uygur is set to formally endorse the California Democrat on Thursday night during his annual appearance on nephew Hasan Piker's Twitch stream, a Thanksgiving Day debate-a-thon the pair call "Cenksgiving." Uygur told POLITICO he will pitch Khanna as the best populist progressive candidate. His Rebellion PAC will also debut its first 2028 ad promoting a Khanna candidacy Thursday night. "For me, it's a no-brainer," Uygur said in an interview, explaining why he’s backing Khanna. "Who else would you back, and why would any progressive or any populist back anyone else?" Along with his PAC getting behind Khanna, Uygur is also launching his own "Draft Ro" website to collect signatures and showcase other early high-profile endorsers, though he wouldn't say who just yet. The endorsement is one of the first of the 2028 cycle, and it comes before any major candidate has formally announced. Inside Washington, Khanna’s chances are viewed as quite slim. But for Uygur, that kind of underestimation is exactly part of the draw. "I love it," Uygur said of the skepticism. "I wouldn't have backed him if anyone in D.C. was behind him." "We're running against Washington," he added. "So if Washington doesn't like a candidate, perfect." Uygur is pairing his endorsement with a litmus test he’s trying to lay down for 2028 progressives: Candidates must call what Israel has done in Gaza a genocide and support ending U.S. funding for Israel. "It isn't actually about Israel," Uygur said. "It's about: Is this person going to represent us or not?" Khanna, he said, is "among the very, very few, and maybe the only candidate, that'll pass that test." He allowed for one other: "There's also AOC. If she runs, that's another person that could pass the test." But that's as far as the praise goes. His endorsement of Khanna comes as many other progressives are waiting to see whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) jumps in. Uygur isn't one of them. Asked if her entry would change his calculus, he said: "Not 1%." "Sorry, but I don't think AOC means it," he said. "I don't think she would do any of the things that she says, and so I'm not going to back someone who is not going to deliver." "She's obsessed with the establishment, so she's going to run a soft, weak race," he added. "She wants to make Democratic leaders and mainstream media happy. Good luck with that strategy." Khanna has told POLITICO he plans to decide whether to run after the holidays and that whether Ocasio-Cortez gets in won't factor into his decision. Uygur's backing could give the potential 2028 candidate some credibility on the populist left, not to mention a boost from "The Young Turks," one of the longest-running and most popular progressive shows online, which Uygur launched in 2002. He also co-founded Justice Democrats in 2017 and ran a long-shot bid of his own for the 2024 Democratic presidential nomination. His Rebellion PAC sparked controversy during the 2026 midterms with an ad tying U.S. funding for Israel to higher grocery prices, which the campaign of then-Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced itself from. Uygur, who was also a prominent backer of Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential runs, has a blunt prediction for 2028: "I'm positive Ro Khanna is going to win."

items.originalTitle: How to Have a More Sustainable Black Friday, According to Experts
items.author: Simmone Shah
items.title: How to Have a More Sustainable Black Friday, According to Experts
items.summary: Black Friday signage displayed in a retail window on Oxford Street on Nov. 23, 2026 in London, England. —Alishia Abodunde—Getty Images Black Friday is here—holding the promise of good deals and the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season. But if you plan to shop the sales, take the time to think about what you really need —and what you plan to give. Americans spent $10 billion dollars on unwanted gifts in 2024. And last year, 65% of consumers reported returning a holiday gift, while 54% admitted to regifting an unwanted item. So, being more intentional about your holiday shopping can benefit both your wallet and the planet. “We are in an era right now where things are very expensive , and so when we're talking about affordability and Black Friday, thinking about what's really going to serve us and make us happy is a great way of thinking about sustainability too,” says Shelie Miller co-director of the Center for Sustainable Systems at the University of Michigan. “Being thoughtful about what's happening to our bank accounts as well as the overall amount of stuff we're buying can be very helpful as far as guiding us to a better path forward.” We spoke with experts about how best to avoid overconsumption and shop with sustainability in mind this Black Friday. Plan your shopping—and stick to the list Before you shop, create a list of what you’re looking for to avoid any unwanted impulse purchases. “Having a list and sticking to it can be helpful for curbing some of those impulsive consumptions when that impulsivity is sky high,” says Karen Winterich, professor of marketing at Penn State University. When you’re shopping, think twice before jumping on any deals for items that weren’t on your list. “We often get sucked into buying because it feels like a good deal,” says Winterich. “It makes us feel good to get that deal, and then later we may actually feel regret. Like, ‘I got a good deal, but did I even need to buy in the first place?’” To avoid feeling any regret, focus on how much you’re spending rather than how much you’re saving. “Even if we're saving a lot, we're still spending,” says Winterich. “If it's 90% off, but I don't need it, I'm not going to use it. Don't buy it.” Be intentional with your gifts If you’re buying gifts for the holiday season, take some time to think about the person you’re shopping for before you swipe your card. “If you're buying for someone else, pause and think about the person and if [the gift] is something they would really want and enjoy and use, or if you’re buying it to check the box, and say, ‘I got them a gift,’” says Winterich. If you know your friend has a cupboard full of coffee mugs, consider getting them locally roasted coffee beans or treating them to a coffee instead of buying them another mug. Consider gifting something people can consume—especially if you’re buying for someone you don’t know very well, like an office Secret Santa or a new neighbor. “Maybe that’s a loaf of local bread or something you make yourself with a locally made jam, or it could be some hot chocolate mix with a special treat attached to it,” says Winterich. “Something that's consumable and not necessarily made from plastics and shipped overseas, but a little bit more locally made, that they're going to consume and not have sitting around or donating. [It conveys] ‘I'm still thinking of you, I'm still giving you a gift, but it's not stuff that is going to sit there that you’re not going to enjoy and appreciate.” Consider your footprint Individual actions may not seem like much, but their impact can add up. Every year, people in the United States throw out more than 34 billion lbs of used textiles— roughly 100 lbs of textile waste per person each year—while global electronic waste continues to climb . If you’re buying an item online, see if you can pick it up at the store. Last mile delivery, the final step before a product reaches your doorstop, is responsible for roughly half of a delivery’s total emissions. “If you know you're already going to be going to the store, maybe you could just pick out one day in the week and say I'm going to hit these couple stores up where I have items to pick up at, rather than having that individual last mile delivery,” says Winterich. Consider shopping for quality rather than quantity—and be mindful of what you might already have at home. “A lot of times with impulse buys we're trying to get as much stuff for as little money as possible,” says Miller. “When we're talking about sustainability, we want people to use items for a long time to get their best environmental value.” “Everything that we buy had [manufacturing and shipping] impacts that were many times bigger than the product itself,” continues Miller. “So [thinking] maybe that stocking stuffer isn't really going to bring joy, and it's just going to affect my pocketbook. That actually has some environmental [benefits] to it.”

items.originalTitle: Why You Should Train to Be Ethically Fit
items.author: David W. Miller and Susan Richardson
items.title: Why You Should Train to Be Ethically Fit
items.summary: —oxygen—Getty Images Think of great athletes; they are fit in a way that relies on years of training and practice. An accomplished track star did not suddenly decide to run the four-minute mile one morning and have all the skills, strength, and endurance to do it. Elite tennis players prepare for and anticipate mid-game scenarios and know just what shot to draw on because they’ve practiced it thousands of times. Or think of great musicians who are fit because they’ve practiced scales, arpeggios, and studies for years before they perform a challenging work. A brilliant cellist did not suddenly decide to play the Bach cello suites one morning and have it artfully under her fingers immediately. They have cultivated their ability by keeping the skills going all along. In each case, they developed and practiced their skills—their fitness or wellness, so to speak—over time so they would be ready when they’re playing in pressure-packed moments under the bright lights. Our research and experience convince us that we can become and stay ethically fit by cultivating ethical strength and agility so that, when the moment comes, the muscle patterns and range of motion we need are there. The question for many then becomes how to get those muscles and then keep them in shape. You could certainly delve into the great classical schools of ethics, reading in-depth tomes by thinkers past and present. You could probe the great ancient spiritual and religious traditions for their wisdom on the human struggle with right and wrong and the practices that can help. You could read policies and laws related to ethics, which would easily take up multiple volumes (and lots of time). Or you might look to recent psychological and neurological studies on the way our brains work and why, realizing the “right” thing may be trickier than we think. These are all great things to do… if you have the time and the bandwidth. But for many of us, life’s demands mean that instead, we need to harvest the core ideas from all these traditions and craft an intellectually robust, informed, and practical set of ethical tools while also cultivating the strength to wield them. You can move from simply having knowledge—the ethical exercises—to having wisdom, a reflective way of looking at decisions in your life and indeed at yourself. I hope that as you think about what success looks like in your life, and what you want it to look like in the future, such wisdom will be part of it. Life is all about decisions, in which we act out—and often find out—who we are. There are a range of ways to think about how ethics works in our lives. But given how decisions both draw on who we’ve been and shape who we’re becoming, we’ll focus here on decision-making as an elevated moment in the ethical landscape of our lives. How we want to see ourselves as behaving and how we actually behave in the moment, or our “lived ethic,” can all too easily be two different things. As you reflect honestly on your recent decisions, what is your own lived ethic? What is mine? And how can it be wiser and more informed for the sake of your future self and those you care about? Experiences from the past, things in the moment that can throw us off balance, and an unrealistic sense of the future can make a sound ethical decision difficult to discern. What we need are the tools and practices for effectively tackling ethical decisions, particularly when the dilemma is in the ethical gray zone or, worse, disguised and unrecognizable until it is too late. Ethics is not simply about laws and compliance. Rather, it’s also about character (yours) and culture (your organization’s). This is not to take away from compliance officers and departments; indeed, hopefully, it will affirm their importance as one place in the larger picture. Compliance departments and guidelines are necessary but not sufficient. They tend to look backward, focused on catching those who’ve violated laws and regulations, whereas ethics understood as character and culture is focused on avoiding future mistakes. Law, codes, and policy are an important place to begin, but we need to use other ethical perspectives as well. Similarly, ethics is not merely about telling people to be “good” or “moral,” an approach that can be misleading and unhelpful. First, telling someone just to “be moral” can put inordinate pressure on them without giving them the tools they need to fulfill the expectation. And telling people to be good can also be interpreted in too many ways. More helpful is an approach that helps you identify ethical problems as such and know your own ethical sources and tools for making an ethical decision. Such an approach helps you better imagine possible outcomes, either positive or negative, and see yourself working through them. But if ethics isn’t only about compliance or the admonition to be good, then what else is it? My view is that it also gathers the two critical pieces of character and culture, which in turn invite deeper questions. What shapes and sustains your individual character or the corporate culture of the business or organization you’re a part of? What role (if any) do religious or spiritual traditions play in either one? For many, their faith tradition—even if they move away from the doctrinal claims or practices—remains influential, if not central, to their ethical grounding and sense of societal responsibility. What other sources or reality checks do you use in ethical decision-making—a mentor, for instance, or a close family member you check in with? How carefully do you track and trust your intuition and gut instinct? Your lived ethic is the behavior and values you personally bring into an ethical decision. But the fact is you’re never there alone. You are in an ethical field, which can be compared with a playing field in sports. That field comprises the context in which your personal ethics and decision-making is taking place, including external factors, organizational ethics, and the ethics of other people. For ethical decisions, we are rarely solo actors. Excerpted from T he 5 Questions for Ethical Decisions: How to Succeed Without Selling Your Soul by David W. items.title: A bakery, a playground, a speaker’s corner … how a former Brussels car garage tore up the art gallery rulebook
items.summary: Repurposing a space previously used for selling Citroëns, the Belgian capital now has its first ever dedicated space for contemporary art. It’s certainly ambitious – but will they be able to fill it? ‘A cathedral of cars” is how the colossal Citroën garage in Brussels was described when it opened in 1934, conceived as a startling glass temple to showcase the streamlined wonders of the automobile age. It greeted the street with an immense curtain wall of glass that wrapped a monumental nave-like showroom, culminating in a curved art deco prow, which glowed like a crystal lantern by night. Almost a century later, arts and culture have replaced cars as the great urban consumables of our age. Consequently, after a €230m decade-long transformation in collaboration with the Pompidou Centre, this gargantuan garage has been reborn as a palace of performance, dance, music, film, architecture and visual art. The original Parisian Pompidou was designed as a transformable cultural machine for the city ; this place takes those urban ambitions to an even greater extreme.

items.summary: It’s early days, but after a dramatic roster overhaul and an offseason of team-bonding Dončić is playing at an MVP level and LA are looking like contenders One of the components of Luka Dončić’s shock trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Los Angeles Lakers that caused great consternation was that he was just entering his prime as an NBA superstar. The worry was that the move could end that prime before it really even began – unceremoniously uprooting the Slovenian wunderkind from a team custom built around his strengths, fresh off a run to the NBA finals, to one who didn’t really make sense at all. Sure, the bright lights of Hollywood would elevate Dončić’s profile and usher him into a new echelon of stardom. But with Oklahoma City starting their run of dominance and rising stars around the league waiting in the wings, some believed his hopes of title contention (or even a long-elusive MVP award) had vanished. But the start to this season raises the question: what if they were wrong? Dončić is neck-and-neck with Victor Wembanyama in the MVP race, and the Lakers have the best record in the NBA at 15-3, with the Spurs and 76ers just behind at 15-4. San Antonio and their gargantuan French superstar were title and MVP favorites by a wide margin entering this season. But Dončić and the Lakers are keeping pace by pretty much every margin. Friday night’s NBA Cup showdown will be a duel with ripple effects and stakes rarely seen in the regular season, let alone in November. The two top records. The two leading MVP candidates. A basketball fan couldn’t ask for much more.

items.title: ‘I’m like a lamp-post. Not glam, but vital’: Jennifer Reid, the singer saving the Industrial Revolution’s working-class songs
items.summary: She started out scribbling 19th-century workers’ songs on receipts at her retail job. Now, the folk disruptor is taking them global – and finding resonances with today’s injustices When Jennifer Reid was working in Home Bargains, she used till receipts to write out the folk ballads she was learning by heart, and then tucked them into her waistband, because staff uniforms didn’t have pockets. “Or if it was too sweaty in summer, I’d hide them behind the shampoo bottles and then go back for them,” she recalls. Growing up in Middleton, Greater Manchester, Reid discovered local broadside ballads – single-sheet songs sold on the street depicting life and events, which boomed during the Industrial Revolution – when volunteering at Chetham’s Library in her late teens. Reid describes her years prior to this as being “a cantankerous young ’un with all this energy that was sometimes misdirected into antisocial stuff” but this new direction was mind-expanding. “I’d never thought about Oldham or Rochdale in a historical cultural context before,” she says. “Very soon I realised: I want to make sure this history doesn’t die.”

items.summary: Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down By Stacy Kranitz @media only screen and (min-width: 767px) { .wp-block-image:not(.alignright,.alignleft,:has(.block-editor-media-placeholder)) { margin: 3rem 1rem 1rem 1rem; } } Nonfiction More than just a photobook, Stacy Kranitz’s latest work shows her pushing further into the role of historian, offering a rich visual history of the mountainous areas of Kentucky, Ohio, Tennessee, and West Virginia—Appalachia. It’s a region with a complicated story, often mistold by outsiders. Kranitz weaves together historical images with photos from her own extensive archive from decades of living and working there. She doesn’t glorify and doesn’t shy away from the harsh life many of its inhabitants face. Some of the historical images are paired uncannily with Kranitz’s own recent photos—poses, locations, and expressions mirroring each other almost 100 years apart. Kranitz frames the book around the writings of Harry Caudill, a lawyer from Eastern Kentucky who inspired President Lyndon B. Johnson’s “war on poverty.” Following the failure of the “war” in Appalachia, Caudill became disillusioned and changed his thinking, coming to believe that the Appalachian gene pool had been “watered down by inbreeding among what he called ‘dullards.’” Kranitz addresses Caudill’s own conflicted and complicated legacy head-on. If you take the book at face value, you have an interesting and fun romp through the mountains and hollers of Appalachia. If you spend more time and dig deeper, just as Kranitz has done, you’ll discover an investigation of complex questions about photography’s role in representation and stereotyping, as well as the relationship among a photographer, her subjects, and the viewer taking them in. — Mark Murrmann Buy It Here American Hagwon By Min Jin Lee Fiction I started reading this novel when I was fact-checking my colleague Inae Oh’s wonderful profile of Min Jin Lee and found I couldn’t put the book down. Centered on the Kohs, a middle-class Korean family pushed to immigrate across continents due to economic pressures before landing in the United States, the story is a powerful meditation on familial love, duty, and what it means to live a meaningful life, through the lens of education. What keeps impressing me about Lee’s work is the compassionate, complicated, and wise way in which she writes all of her characters. We feel their betrayal, loss, grief, sacrifice, and fortitude as though we were experiencing it ourselves. Lee spent almost 10 years conducting research for this book, going to hagwons (for-profit tutoring centers) in South Korea and Southern California and having conversations with hundreds of parents, teachers, and children (including, I later realized, one of my friends), and you can tell how much care and attention she put into listening to everyone’s experiences. — Mariana Duran Buy on Bookshop The Author Weekend By Laura Zigman Fiction Among the seemingly endless ways the world divides during these fractious times, let me add one that is singularly nonpartisan: mystery lovers versus those who aren’t. I’m usually in the latter category—all the plot twists confuse me, so even the weakest Big Reveal tends to leave me slack-jawed with shock, and with the creeping sense that I’m dumb. Plus, in this violent world, do I really want to read about murders for pleasure? So with this slightly defensive preface, let me answer with a resounding yes, and that’s because of the new mystery by the often laugh-out-loud funny, always socially insightful, and compulsively readable Laura Zigman. I was drawn to The Author Weekend, not just because I am such a fan (and yes, friend) of Zigman’s or because of its flap-copy framing as “ The Devil Wears Prada meets The White Lotus .” (What’s not to like?) My catnip was the organizing principle of the narrative: an almost has-been, middle-aged female writer struggling desperately, indeed too desperately, to survive in an utterly unforgiving publishing industry, which Zigman knows extremely well. She used to work on the inside—a perspective she brings with lacerating clarity—and is an author and ghostwriter. Here is a delightful opportunity to luxuriate in high-level gossip, the hatchet-faced betrayals, and the ruthless algorithm that informs the decision-making of who will make it and who will be discarded like yesterday’s New York Post. Yes, a real murder mystery resides at the heart of The Author Weekend, which mystery aficionados are bound to appreciate. But for the rest of us mere civilians, this book is truly a can’t-go-to-sleep-without-reading-the-next-chapter delight. — Marianne Szegedy-Maszak Buy on Bookshop Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State By Michael Lewis Nonfiction Ever since 1989’s Liar’s Poker , I’ve been hooked on the work of Michael Lewis, whose superpower is finding memorable characters to illuminate broader themes. There’s no shortage of them in Blockers , a great read, though the organizing principal theme—“blockers” being civil servants who resisted President Donald Trump’s agenda—mainly felt like an excuse to cobble together profiles of seven fascinating career employees drummed out of government by Trump’s mindless minions. People like Tim Curry, a soft-spoken Office of Personnel Management employee so uniquely valuable that a co-worker calls him a “bus person”—meaning if he were hit by a bus, “the government would stop working.” And Kathleen Walters, who as the IRS’s chief privacy officer was charged with ensuring all of our personal data stays locked down. There’s a long chapter on Alex Maranghides, a maverick in an obscure Department of Commerce unit who became a sought-after expert on how wildfires behave—probably too long a chapter, though I’ll never again look at my neighbor’s fence the same way. Blockers is the latest of four Lewis books featuring, directly or indirectly, some of the unexpected and preternaturally dedicated oddballs who forged a path in government, often working for offices few people have ever heard of. Our civil service provides a seemingly endless font of characters for the enterprising nonfiction writer. It’s just a shame so many are now emeritus. —Michael Mechanic Buy on Bookshop The Conspiracists: Women, Extremism, and the Lure of Belonging By Noelle Cook Nonfiction At this point, the January 6 insurrection almost feels like a fever dream. Noelle Cook was there that day in 2021, taking pictures for a visual anthropology project she hoped to do. Looking around, she had an uncomfortable observation: She was not alone. There were women everywhere, many of them middle-aged white women who looked a lot like her. The Conspiracists takes you past snappy headlines and bizarre social media clips into the everyday lives of two women—Yvonne, an ex-Marine and grandmother of 11, and Tammy, a divorcée and recovering addict who used QAnon conspiracies to cope during the pandemic—who were prosecuted for their roles in January 6 and kept falling farther down the rabbit hole. It’s fascinating to get inside their heads and hear how they make sense of their “conspirituality.” Rather than gawking at the women in one or two shocking interviews, Cook becomes part of their lives over several years and develops theories about the “gendered pathways of radicalization,” pointing at how the lack of space for middle-aged women in right-wing ideals or imagery pushes these women to conspiracy communities where they can have a voice. As we head into the back half of Trump’s second term and these ideas keep taking root in the electorate, The Conspiracists offers a unique insight into what motivates this kind of person and how the need for community underlies it. — Gabriella Gladney Buy on Bookshop Found Sound By Meg Wolitzer and Charlie Panek Fiction Felix Frank is feeling tuned out, unsatisfied by the rhythms of childhood, annoyed by his genius kid brother, and stuck in the doldrums of the tween years. Found Sound starts with yet another summer stay in western Massachusetts for Felix’s family. But despite the familiar surroundings, something is missing these days. Felix feels pangs of longing and anger for his older brother Dylan, who blazed a trail and seemed to burn bridges. Nothing has been the same at home since he left. Next-door neighbor Marigold is a little weird, but she makes life more interesting. A friendship forms as clues start to pile up…but for what? Hidden recordings, secret messages from DJs, and a place no one is supposed to visit in the basement capture Felix and Marigold’s imaginations, and a quest is on. Found Sound is a breezy, fun read built to entertain lovers of young adult fiction, mystery fans, audiophiles, and those who still geek out over radio. And the authors of this scavenger hunt come by it honestly: Wolitzer is the host of public radio’s Selected Shorts , and Panek, her son, is a musician and sound designer. Their authentic love for audio and the science of sound flows through the pages, in depictions of anechoic chambers and cassette-tape memories. As an added bonus, the “How to Get Started With Found Sound” note at the end invites readers young and old to make their own audio projects, with a few helpful tips for beginners. — Jim Briggs Buy on Bookshop John of John By Douglas Stuart Fiction Every time I opened this book, the rushing world around me came to a halt. There I was, on a dirt road overlooking a windswept croft on a remote Scottish island, where nearby, one of the titular characters sits hunched over his loom, weaving tweed. Cal (officially John-Calum Macleod, son of John Macleod) has answered a call to return home from the mainland after failing to nab a job post-uni. He is broke, horny, and not all that enthused to be living again under the gaze of his father, a stern and hardworking Calvinist churchgoer. Cal has more fun shooting the shit with his maternal grandmother, an eccentric bird who holds the tenancy papers to the croft (agricultural property) where they all reside. Raising sheep and handweaving tartans—it’s difficult work that no longer pays enough, and everyone’s health is deteriorating. But if this premise sounds at all stodgy, know that this novel brims with flirtations, love affairs, pub gossip, betrayals, and layers upon layers of secrets. Stuart, who won the Booker Prize for his 2020 debut novel, Shuggie Bain , threads in Gaelic dialogue and piercing descriptions of the rugged Isle of Harris. Against the backdrop of the black-green sea, he masterfully renders his passionate, stubborn characters, allowing us to fully inhabit the relationships and longings that sustain them and erode them. — Maddie Oatman Buy on Bookshop Lifeguard: A Love Story By Janet Fash Nonfiction Janet Fash is a working-class gal from Prospect Park who fell in love with the ocean. But this story is not Baywatch ; Lifeguard is both a campy Rockaway Beach memoir as well as a serious contribution to the feminist canon. Fash reads the audiobook herself, and in her thick Brooklyn accent, she describes the early days of her career in the 1970s, when seasoned lifeguards would haze new recruits by covering them in paint or ketchup or, in the case of one of Fash’s friends, chasing her into the water and stripping her naked. She parties at the local beach bars with the mostly male lifeguards and occasionally shows them up by swimming faster. But she’s also singularly focused on saving lives. During her climb through the ranks to become New York City’s first female chief lifeguard, Fash witnesses harrowing drownings and near-misses, especially in poorer areas where people are less likely to know how to swim. She is radicalized when she realizes that many of the deaths could have been prevented by better-trained guards. She butts heads with colleagues who fall asleep on the chair or don’t watch the water but are protected by union bosses. The malfeasance had deadly consequences. In one lawsuit against the city, a jury awarded $2 million to the families of two Black boys who drowned in 1990 after one of those incompetent guards—dubbed the “Angel of Death” by his colleagues—responded to a plea for help by saying, “If they can’t fucking swim, then why did they come to the beach?” Fash details her fight against deeply entrenched sexism and a corrupt union boss to improve conditions for both lifeguards and swimmers. Her book is an unusual window into New York City politics, told by a woman in a swimsuit who spoke truth to power. — Stephanie Mencimer Buy on Bookshop Precisely Now By Lawrence Joseph Poetry When life seems especially perilous, some poems and poets encapsulate the anguish of the period. Think T. S. Eliot and the “Waste Land” after the devastation of World War I. Or Allen Ginsberg’s poetic disgust with the conformity of the 1950s in “Howl .” Or the young Amanda Gorman at President Joe Biden’s surreal post-insurrection, mid-pandemic inauguration, reciting her poem “The Hill We Climb.” Poets can either disappear and immerse in the details of their interior lives, or burst forth, fist shaking, at the coarse and inequitable world around them. Lawrence Joseph, poet, essayist, lawyer, and retired law professor at St. Joseph’s University, is the latter. In his newest collection, Joseph combines the full force of his intellectual rigor with his vast command of the classics, religion, law, culture, and two of America’s iconic cities: Detroit, where he, an Arab American, was born and raised, and New York, where he has lived for decades. This is a book whose rhythms and observations on mass deportations, “plutocratic thievery,” sycophants and enablers, and “permanent war, permanent crisis/whatever you wish to call it” somehow linger in rhythm and cadence, long after you read the poems, like the persistent melody of a song whose words you’ve forgotten. We are relentlessly assaulted by demands on our shredded attention, but do yourself a favor and sit for an hour with this slim volume of verse. You will get to know a singular poet who expresses the fury you can’t and sees what’s hiding in plain sight. And somehow manages, even in his rage, to do it with love. — Marianne Szegedy-Maszak Buy on Bookshop The Rouse By China Miéville Fiction When China Miéville started The Rouse , Trump was hosting The Apprentice ; the president was George W. Bush. And the accretion of 20 years is palpable, both in the book’s complexity and its sheer volume: It is 1,320 pages, spanning more than 50 years, 20 countries, and two complex, radically different lives. The Rouse does much of its work in a barrage of allusions and accounts, largely concerned with imperialism and the paranormal and their intertwining. And not all of it is speculative: A report on “supernatural counterinsurgency in the Congo” briefly mentioned came out of a real study funded by the Pentagon . Two characters’ arcs alternate through most of the novel, and as heady as the novel gets, it is always tethered to meaningful stakes. Reading it felt like seeing a Sleep No More adaptation of real life, more curated if not more legible, and above all, haunted. It begins with a social realist narrative of a single mother in the 1970s. But it reaches the weirdest peaks that any of Miéville’s novels ever has and on the way traverses the Malayan Emergency, Congolese independence, The Troubles, and war, and war, and war. I have gladly read it twice, and once along with the audiobook, which I highly recommend. It asks much of the reader, but it repays manifold. — Melissa Lewis Buy on Bookshop Switzy By Emma Cline Fiction In the last remaining days before death, with your memory fading from Alzheimer’s, what would you prioritize? What would you say and to whom? These final confrontations form the trajectory of Switzy, Emma Cline’s third novel, whose central character is an elderly man with dementia traveling to Switzerland for a self-assisted suicide. It’s undoubtedly a heavy subject and somewhat of a heel turn for Cline, whose earlier fiction tended to involve younger, more wayward subjects. But Switzy doesn’t indulge in the saccharine, nor does it ever sag into the overly philosophical. Instead, Cline’s prose kept impressing me with its machine-like ability to spit out lines that at once portrayed the fracturing of a mind and maintained a nihilistic sense of humor about what it means to be alive in the first place. This is a book that reminds us that our memories are embarrassingly flawed, with or without dementia. That we don’t know our loved ones nearly as well as we think, and vice versa. That no matter how much money you throw at it, closure might always elude us. Which all might seem depressing, and maybe it is! But I ended Switzy with a distinct grin. In the age of endless optimization and fine-tuning, sometimes it’s comforting to be reminded that every one of us ends up in the same exact pit. — Inae Oh Buy on Bookshop The Tuxedo Society By Paul Rudnick Fiction Leave it to playwright Paul Rudnick to recast 007 as a gay man with a secret society. Reggie is a Navy SEAL who was kicked out of the military because of “don’t ask, don’t tell.” When a more enlightened president tries to lure him back into the armed forces, he instead demands the right to assemble an undercover counterespionage team from all the “bravest and most capable queer operatives he could find, to make a point.” The Tuxedo Society’s members hail from every possible gay stereotype. There’s the florist who supervises installations at the White House and Swiss chalets where major bitcoin deals go down. There’s also an Olympic diver and the narrator, a struggling actor who sells candles at the mall. Rudnick turns stereotypes into superpowers, because after all, who makes a better spy than someone the world often doesn’t see? As the florist explains, he’s good at his job because no one finds him threatening. “I’m just a silly homo waltzing in with 18 boxes of calla lilies and birch branches.” The underestimated Tuxes deftly dispatch assassins in men’s rooms and disrupt evil plots to take over the world. Villains include a deliciously rendered Lindsey Graham–like Southern politician and a hypocritical prosperity preacher. This book is campy, the plot is harebrained, the jokes are raunchy. But I’ve been recommending it to people all year because The Tuxedo Society is just so much fun . — Stephanie Mencimer Buy on Bookshop Nonfiction and Fiction Written Before 2026 The Antidote (2025) By Karen Russell Fiction It takes a while to figure out what the heck is going on in the opening of this fantastically inventive and thought-provoking novel from the author of Swamplandia! and other works of fiction. Suffused with magical realism, the story is, at its heart, a meditation on memory. It is set in Uz, a fictional rural Nebraska town besieged by the blinding storms and crop devastation of the Dust Bowl. It features a sadistic sheriff; a semi-aware scarecrow; an anxious wheat farmer and his strong-headed 15-year-old niece, still coming to terms with her mother’s murder; a young Black New Deal photographer shocked to discover that her Graflex camera is capturing images of the region’s past and (perhaps) future; and the titular “prairie witch,” who has taken “the Antidote” as her trade name. She’s one of a far-flung community of “vaults,” shunned women who earn their living by banking people’s memories without any awareness of the dark secrets they harbor inside. Times are challenging in Uz, and strange occurrences are aplenty as Karen Russell ushers her readers toward a dreadful awareness of what we stand to gain, and lose, when we pick and choose our memories. Compellingly written and girded by nonfictional events—namely the systematic displacement and extermination of Native Americans on the prairie—that some may prefer not to remember, The Antidote winds up being hard to forget. —Michael Mechanic Buy on Bookshop Fish Tales (1983/2025) By Nettie Jones Fiction “Weird girl” literature has become synonymous, rightly or wrongly, with a certain navel-gazing, city-dwelling, modern woman (usually white) who isn’t afraid to be, well, gross. But long before there was any kind of realized canon, Nettie Jones’ debut was the rare novel that dared to paint a complicated Black woman in full light. First published in 1983 to little fanfare, the book has found new life, republished last year by Farrar, Straus and Giroux. It owes its revival largely to renewed attention to the late Toni Morrison ’s career as an editor at Random House. Fish Tales was one of the books she championed, and it’s easy to see why. Morrison, always concerned with the full breadth of Black women’s complications, likely found Jones’ honest, mostly autobiographical portrayal of a woman caught up in the fabulous New York underground scene in the ’70s refreshing. While the story deals vaguely with the trauma protagonist Lewis Jones endures, it largely avoids coming off as a cautionary tale thanks to raw, visceral language that presents her story without judgment, but with plenty of deviant sex, drug use, parties, and uncomfortable reckonings with what it means to look for connection. Reading it this past summer made me think, “Man, I’ve gotta live more.” —Gabriella Gladney Buy on Bookshop James (2024) By Percival Everett Fiction You don’t need to have read Mark Twain’s The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn to be completely immersed in Percival Everett’s James , a unique retelling of Twain’s classic adventure tale. Everett’s award-winning 2024 novel is as riveting as any thriller, told through the eyes of the enslaved man known in the original story as Jim as he and Huck make their way down the Mississippi River. James reminded me of another novel I read and loved this year: Demon Copperhead , Barbara Kingsolver’s fictional story of a young man growing up in opioid-addled contemporary Appalachia, which was inspired by another classic coming-of-age tale, Charles Dickens’ David Copperfield . Both reimaginings are beautiful tributes to the stories that inspired them, updated for a new generation of readers. Both follow characters with rich inner worlds. Both are deeply moving stories, in part, about family, friendship, and resistance in a world that refuses to acknowledge the full humanity of its most vulnerable. James is also a story about the transformative and revolutionary power of education, with an ending that’s extremely cathartic. You won’t want to put it down. —Chasity Hale Buy on Bookshop The Journalist and the Murderer (1990) By Janet Malcolm Nonfiction If you liked You Can See Everything , this is a must-read. It’s co-director Lance Oppenheim’s favorite book and a powerful reflection on journalism ethics, voyeurism, and the reasons we decide people are guilty and worthy of moral punishment. The story centers on journalist Joe McGinniss, who agrees to write a novel about a man on trial for the murder of his wife and daughters, per the defendant’s request. The book he eventually publishes clearly frames the accused as guilty, and the (now-convicted) murderer sues McGinniss for misleading (and befriending) him during the reporting process and betraying his trust. I love how author Janet Malcolm writes and how she tries to understand the motivations of everyone she talks to. She’s not afraid to ask her subjects or her audience to wrestle with harsh conclusions or field difficult questions, including whether certain people, simply because society may view them as abhorrent, are less deserving than others of transparency and professionalism—a notion those in our field would do well to revisit from time to time. — Mariana Duran Buy on Bookshop Kindred (1979) By Octavia E. Butler Fiction I never gravitated toward science fiction until Octavia E. Butler whacked me over the head with it. Perhaps best known for Parable of the Sower and Parable of the Talents —her devastating and eerily prescient duology of 1990s dystopian novels about a mid-2020s climate-ravaged society—Butler writes with such unflinching clarity about the brutal realities of our time that it’s easy to forget she’s making it up. Kindred is a similarly harrowing read, but rather than launch into some hypothetical near-future, it catapults readers into the past. Main character Dana, a Black woman in 1970s California, is repeatedly transported back to the antebellum South, where she encounters her Black—and white—relatives and the horrors of slavery. What struck me about Dana is that, while she focuses on staying alive and keeping her family together, she often must sacrifice her dignity in the process. She’s imperfect, and her knowledge of the future hurts her as much as it helps her, but Dana’s empathy and depth is what I loved most about her. The book is haunting and honest, and Butler has you believing her premise from the very first page. In archival tape aired 15 years after she died, she talked about reading science fiction as a girl and realizing that none of the authors looked like her. I hope others are as moved as I was by Butler’s deft use of the genre to explore America’s racial history and themes of power, class, and survival. —Rachel Santarsiero Buy on Bookshop Legacy of Ashes: The History of the CIA (2007) By Tim Weiner Nonfiction It’s all right there in the title. Tim Weiner’s Bush-era epic is an 848-page doorstopper with one unmistakable throughline: Just about everything The Agency has ever done has blown up in its face. I can’t say I was caught off guard by this conclusion—everyone who has ever recommended this book to me has described it in more or less this same way—but the hubris and incompetence and Yale-ness on display is overwhelming all the same. This is not some vamped-up Wikipedia entry; Weiner obtained tens of thousands of documents and tracked down old spooks to piece together hidden histories of the CIA’s Cold War escapades. He paints a picture of an often hapless agency that, far from its Hollywood myth-making, has long struggled to justify its existence. But hey, at least the days of reckless regime change in Iran are safely in our past, right? —Tim Murphy Buy on Bookshop Letters and Papers from Prison (1951) By Dietrich Bonhoeffer Nonfiction Gestapo prisons and concentration camps are far from the ideal place to wrestle with Jesus’ call for the modern world, but that’s where Lutheran pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer found himself for two years before Hitler ordered him executed. His reflections on the role of Christianity in society, though sadly half-formed at points, feel especially relevant as our Defense Department invokes the Prince of Peace in unprecedented terms. We are fighting the Iran war not just in America’s name, but also in the name of God—who Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says “trains our hands for war,” “break[s] the teeth of the ungodly,” and helps deliver “overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy.” I don’t know which god he’s referring to— Moloch ?—but that description bears little resemblance to the God made incarnate in the Gospels. It certainly isn’t the one Bonhoeffer knew, who helps us “not by his omnipotence…but by his weakness and suffering.” Bonhoeffer’s writings also feel relevant in this age of AI, with its myriad prophecies of ways the world could become quite inhuman. I took heart in his advice to his fellow Germans, who were living under so much more depravity and suspense than we are now: Pursue “the very narrow way, often extremely difficult to find, of living every day as if it were our last, and yet living in faith and responsibility as though there were to be a great future.” —Satchel Walton Buy on Bookshop Lincoln (1984) By Gore Vidal Fiction The former Minnesota congresswoman Michele Bachmann once said she’d been a Democrat until she read Gore Vidal’s 1973 novel, Burr , and recoiled at its “snotty” depiction of the Founding Fathers. (George Washington is a bad general, Thomas Jefferson is a snake, and Aaron Burr might be Martin Van Buren’s dad.) Burr had a different effect on me: I just wanted to read more Vidal, so I did, and thank God for that. Lincoln , the second book in Vidal’s Narratives of Empire series, is about whom you think. The past year was a good one to read about the man who steered this country through the Civil War, and the portrait therein is as rich and thoughtful as you might hope. But what I really like about it is what Bachmann couldn’t stand, which is just how much Vidal cherishes mess . The ambition of Salmon Chase, Lincoln’s Treasury secretary, is constantly undercut by his anxiety-inducing nearsightedness. John Hay, the president’s youthful aide, cannot stay away from brothels. Mary Todd Lincoln, a woman ahead of her time, loots the Treasury to fund costly White House renovations. Oh, and Honest Abe once had syphilis. Or did he? Many historians disliked this book, not least because of the syphilis. I got the sense that Vidal enjoyed arguing with them almost as much as he enjoyed writing it. Don’t sleep on his 4,686-word letter to the New York Review of Books in response to critics of the book and subsequent mini-series. —Tim Murphy Buy on Bookshop Martyr! (2024) By Kaveh Akbar Fiction How do you live a life worthwhile enough to die with purpose? That’s the question that haunts main character Cyrus Shams in this morbid-yet-hilarious novel about a queer Iranian man wrestling with substance abuse, depression, and the tragic death of his mother in an “accidental” Tehran plane crash. Cyrus is a young poet living in Indiana, and his obsession with death and martyrs forces him to delve into the lives of historical figures and the ghosts of deceased loved ones to make sense of reality. At one point, author Kaveh Akbar writes, “he wanted to live perfectly enough to die without creating a ripple of pain behind him, like an Olympic diver knifing splashlessly into a pool.” Martyr! is suffused with culture—Iranian, American, and Iranian American—all of which Akbar manages to skewer and praise in equal measure as he weaves myriad voices, literary forms, and snippets of archival text into a world more metaphysical than our own. From Cyrus’ insomniac conversations between make-believe characters and dead relatives—a trick he uses to fall asleep—to his spur-of-the-moment trip to Brooklyn to visit a dying Iranian artist doing a performance piece about her death, Martyr! left me breathless. There’s tragedy in this novel, but also joy and poetry and love. I often found myself wanting to cut out lines and keep them safe in my pocket. This novel will change how you talk, how you see. You’ll find yourself bringing it up in conversation without meaning to. I still do. —Rachel Santarsiero Buy on Bookshop The Radicalism of the American Revolution (1992) By Gordon S. Wood Nonfiction Summer 2026 could have been a banner season for a liberal-coded vision of the American idea, with the eyes of the world turned to a cross-continental World Cup as we marked 250 years of independence. I needn’t list the reasons why it was not . Nevertheless, I found myself greatly inspired upon revisiting Gordon S. Wood’s account of the revolutionary era’s egalitarian character. It is easy to forget just how radical it was that, as recent descendants of societies that enforced rigid hierarchies in every facet of life, “ordinary Americans came to believe that no one in a basic down-to-earth and day-in-and-day-out manner was really better than anyone else.” Also notable this year was how clearly the founders saw that republics were “extremely liable to corruption” and demanded virtue from citizens and officeholders—centuries prior to the emergence of pump-and-dump crypto schemes! For those of us raised amid lefty intellectual environments, it is almost second nature to reflect on the shortcomings of the American founding, especially the galling hypocrisy of those who proclaimed universal equality while enslaving their fellow men. But there’s also much to claim and take inspiration from, if we want it. One month before the semiquincentennial, Wood died in an all-too-American way—he was struck by a car in a supermarket parking lot. But the American ideas he chronicled will persist, as Ben Franklin famously put it, if we can keep them. — Satchel Walton Buy on Bookshop var $ = jQuery;$(document).ready(function(){var $area = $('.hero.is-image');var vid = $(' ');$area.find('img').remove();$area.prepend(vid);});

She left the company in 2017 and in March 2025 published a book about her time at Meta. items.originalTitle: Will we ever see another game like GTA VI?
items.author: Dustin DeSoto
items.title: Will we ever see another game like GTA VI?
items.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI arrived last week, 13 years after the last installment in the series, to an enormous debut — nearly $3.8 billion in its first day, according to developer Rockstar Games. That’s more than Avengers: Endgame has earned at the global box office across its entire theatrical run, including rereleases. The game took more than eight years to develop, and Rockstar grew to more than 4,700 employees worldwide during production. In the game, players are catapulted into Leonida, a fictional version of Florida that includes Vice City, the series’ take on Miami. Unlike past games in the series, you play as a couple, Jason and Lucia, who are trying to make enough money to support their young family and make it out. Maintaining their relationship is just as important as robbing stores or completing missions. For all that GTA VI is shaping up to be a critically acclaimed triumph, however, it arrives at a difficult moment for the video game industry. Studios have endured years of layoffs and rising development costs, while workers worry about how generative AI could affect their jobs and creative work. Can an industry under this much pressure afford to keep making games this big, or is GTA VI doomed to be the last of its kind? To find out, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Chris Plante, a video game journalist with about two decades of experience and host of the podcast Post Games . They discussed GTA VI’s long road to release, what could be next for the franchise and whether DLC is on the horizon, and the future of blockbuster gaming more broadly. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify . Chris, people are saying that this game is the last of its kind. Why are they saying that? It kind of is, but I think we should be really specific when we say that. The last of its kind means the last of this: thousands and thousands of people trying to make one game without artificial intelligence, and it being a historic, all-consuming moment. The best shot that we have of another game like this happening is GTA VII. But what I would be wary of is saying there aren’t going to be big-budget video games anymore. If you look at another game that came out just this month, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a remake of one of the most famous games ever, one of the most beloved games ever, and it looks stunning. It’s on the Nintendo Switch 2. It is great. And it cost a fraction of what Grand Theft Auto cost [to make]. It took a fraction of the time to create. And yet it still feels absolutely decadent. You know what a fair comparison would be? We get those Avatar movies — they take forever because they cost a fortune to make, they require all this new technology. That’s your Grand Theft Auto. But you wouldn’t look at an Avatar and say, ‘Well, they’re never going to make expensive movies anymore.’ We still get Dune . We still get Marvel movies. Those things are still happening. There is a whole separate question about the stability of the highest ends of the industry, the companies that tried to be the Grand Theft Autos: Electronic Arts, the company that makes Madden; companies like Xbox, which owns Activision, which makes Call of Duty. You might notice I’m saying a lot of which does this but owns that. The consolidation in the industry is real, and it’s a real problem. So there’s going to be turmoil, but it is not the end of video games, and it’s not even the end of big video games. It sounds like this is a great time for the industry, but it’s actually the opposite. It’s a great time for people who play video games and a nightmare time for people who make video games. If you play video games right now, you can turn on Steam, which is a storefront on PC, and you can find literally hundreds of games that were released just this week. Over a thousand new games are released every month on Steam. And because of that, it targets not every niche, but close. There is probably something out there for you. This is a nightmare for people who make games because even Grand Theft Auto, when it comes to PC, is going to live right alongside all those other games. So for the people who do not have the name recognition, who do not have the marketing, you can launch a game that you spent tens, maybe hundreds of millions of dollars on, and it is going to, the same day that it comes out, compete against a brand-new $5 game that was made by three or four people with a whole bunch of contractor support for a very low cost and has just as good of odds, minus the marketing, of being a hit. Is AI going to make it less risky for big gaming companies to invest in developing something ambitious because maybe they can make it dramatically cheaper and compete with the games that only cost $10 to develop? AI, as the investment class has it in their head: The answer is no, not whatsoever. “Looking even beyond games, there’s a lot of reason to be cautious about things that seem like they’re going to make things faster actually, in the long term, making them much slower.” AI as a tool, it gets more complicated. I think when a lot of people hear AI, they think, I’ve seen a video where I can go on Google and type a prompt, and I say, give me Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but make it like a Black Eyed Peas concert. And people are like, wow, you seem really out of touch, but I’ll make it for you anyway . And then you have this great game, and you are getting the party started in here. And that is not how any of this works at all. Games are literally a miracle. My former colleague, Frank Lantz, who’s an educator and game designer, would compare it to art, if you also had to build a skyscraper or a highway. You have to both make the architecture and make the art. It’s unhinged. We do not have this world where games just are going to materialize. Now where it gets really complicated and it gets really messy inside the industry is using AI tools for things like coding. And this is very controversial amongst a certain corner of video games culture and video game developers. There are people who want a full ban, that we are not using AI on anything, that we need to protect jobs, and that it shouldn’t be used for generating images or art or music or code. And then there are people who say, but I use AI for code. I think it is relatively common, and that is somewhat of a controversial take, but it is what I hear from so many people I talk to who are on that side of game development, to be using it when you are programming as a tool. I think there’s a lot of promises, but I think that, again, looking even beyond games, there’s a lot of reason to be cautious about things that seem like they’re going to make things faster actually, in the long term, making them much slower. And we still live in a world where it makes sense to start developing a GTA VII? It does for Rockstar for sure, though I don’t think that they will be in a rush to do it anytime soon, for a few reasons. One, they still need to get Grand Theft Auto Online out. That’s where the real money is. Grand Theft Auto Online drops people into the city of each new game. Grand Theft Auto V did it with LA. Now you’re going to have it in Miami. And that is where people can get lost for years and years and years, and they can start charging you for little incremental things like cool new outfits or fancy cars or spots to live. So that’s going to be their priority. There has been word or rumor that they might just expand Grand Theft Auto VI, that we would see more cities. Who knows if that’s true? It would be a different approach, but the game began as a thing called Project Americas and was supposed to be a much larger game. So that could be one way that it grows rather than a GTA VII: We just see a GTA VI that gets bigger and bigger, not unlike Fortnite, but we’re going to get more of it. Do you want to put in an early guess as to what year GTA VII comes out so that someone listening to this in, I don’t know, 10, 15, 20 years can be like, wow, that guy nailed it ? Damn. Actually, I was going to say that I think it would be sooner than 13 years, and I’m not sure I actually believe that. I’m going to put it at, let’s say, 2037. I’ll see you in 11 years. Does that sound good? If all goes well for our industries, yes. Yeah. Better odds in the Grand Theft Auto business. I mean, hey, we can always turn into a romantic duo performing a life of crime.

items.originalTitle: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas
items.author: Louis Staples
items.title: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas
items.summary: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist “With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia , which led to a role in Steven Spielberg ’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze , a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’” In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches.

items.originalTitle: The YIMBY Movement’s Greatest Success
items.author: Illustration by Evan Cohen
items.title: The YIMBY Movement’s Greatest Success
items.summary: Berkeley, California, a quintessential university town, may well be the birthplace of anti-growth politics. In 1916, local reformers adopted the country’s first single-family zoning, prohibiting apartments in most residential neighborhoods as a way to exclude disfavored minorities. Progressives would carry on this legacy for the next century in the name of protecting residents from unwanted development. Beginning in the 1960s, housing opponents tried to block construction on environmental grounds—and eventually argued that new residents qualified as “pollution.” Permitting rates were anemic for decades, keeping the city’s population flat even while enrollment at UC Berkeley skyrocketed. Rents and home prices rose accordingly. By the mid-2010s, Berkeley ranked as one of the most expensive college towns in America. But around that time, it began to undergo a remarkable reversal, as students, staff, and young faculty at UC Berkeley came to realize that housing shortages hurt their interests and began working together to push for more inclusive policies. In 2017, they helped organize the group East Bay for Everyone, which showed up constantly to public hearings and helped elect a city council aligned with the “Yes in My Backyard” movement then emerging statewide. With the aid of new state laws loosening zoning requirements—some of which I advocated for as part of my work at YIMBY organizations—permitting of new housing surged. As of 2024, nominal rents barely exceeded 2018 levels, despite inflation. Today Berkeley represents a major success for the YIMBY movement, and it’s not the only one. Across the country, college towns have become boomtowns. As longtime strongholds of progressive politics, their evolution from NIMBY holdouts to YIMBY hotbeds serves as a testament to the left’s shift on housing. If the movement’s next decade is going to deliver on the promise of its first, my fellow housing advocates nationwide will have to replicate the methods that allowed college towns to so quickly build and become more affordable. [ Jonathan Chait: The misguided Democratic opposition to permitting reform ] One obvious lesson is that students and young academics can be persuasive advocates. These groups tend to be temporarily poor and highly social and to have flexible schedules. To put this in criminological terms, they have the motive, means, and opportunity to show up in numbers at the weekday public hearings that determine what does and doesn’t get built. As a result of such activism, once-stagnant college towns across California, including San Luis Obispo and Santa Cruz, have undergone similar transformations as Berkeley: Permitting is up, and rents are starting to stabilize or sometimes even fall. At UC San Diego, campus advocates successfully pushed for new on-campus high-rises that will house thousands of students, helping alleviate the state’s extraordinary rate of student homelessness . In many college towns across the country, off -campus housing is proliferating too: Real-estate-investment trusts, often known as REITs, have plowed billions of dollars into student housing, building roughly 35,000 beds in 2024 alone. According to an estimate from 2020 , some 12 percent of all rental units are for students. Throughout the United States, college towns have taken steps to allow for greater housing density, as Ann Arbor, Michigan, did last month . Perhaps the most extreme example of this is Austin, where the flagship campus of the University of Texas is located. After a decade of trying and failing to overhaul the city zoning code, local YIMBYs began to get their way in the late 2010s, when increasing demand for housing kicked off a construction frenzy. A local backlash grew , threatening to upend the reforms that were turning Greater Austin into America’s fastest-growing metropolis. But YIMBYs were able to preserve their progress thanks in large part to one key group. “When students started to show up to Austin city-council meetings and endorse candidates based on their housing policies, and generally make it clear they want to be viewed as true constituents, it was a game changer,” Felicity Maxwell, a board member of a local pro-housing organization , told me. In 2023, with strong support from local students, lawmakers in Austin were able to sustain the city’s home-building surge by ending both single-family zoning and minimum off-street-parking requirements. The city has been building so much housing that rents are down , even as migration continues to soar. Students and junior academics cannot change decades-old urban-planning habits on their own. Senior faculty have also been instrumental in dislodging a kind of progressivism that treats all development as predatory. Well - respected professors have repeatedly called attention to the need for more housing, drawing on a growing scholarly consensus on the issue. Leaders in more and more college towns have come to see exclusionary housing as incompatible with liberal politics. “I was troubled by the tensions between Ithaca being a progressive, welcoming community that was also staggeringly unaffordable,” Robert Cantelmo, the pro-growth mayor of Ithaca, New York, told me. Cantelmo is a product of Cornell University, where he received a master’s degree and later helped lead a research center. During his tenure, Ithaca has had more active cranes than many far larger American cities. A similar story has played out in Cambridge, Massachusetts. In 2022, a recent MIT grad named Burhan Azeem mobilized students at his alma mater, who in turn helped him become the youngest councilor in the history of the city. Azeem became vice mayor earlier this year and has led a successful campaign to legalize Paris-scale density citywide. [ Read: A perfectly crude way to solve America’s housing shortage ] “Cambridge is one of the youngest towns in Massachusetts, and not just because of undergraduates,” Azeem told me. “A lot of people stay here after graduation, or stay on for years in graduate school, and their big question is, Will I ever be able to buy a home here? That makes for a natural pro-housing constituency.” In some places, however, college communities have limited political influence. At Stanford University, 98 percent of undergraduates live on campus, which is just outside Palo Alto’s municipal limits, leaving them effectively iced out from politics in that city. UC Santa Barbara is located in a county of nearly 500,000 residents, which even the most organized students would struggle to sway. In other college towns, such as Gainesville, Florida, intransigent homeowners and state governments have thwarted reform. Moreover, there are reasons to think that the college-town boom may be short-lived. University enrollment is headed for a death spiral , and dozens of colleges are closing each year. Although flagship universities and elite schools probably won’t close anytime soon, the student body at many institutions will likely shrink. But even if college towns do begin to stagnate, their runaway growth over the past decade has provided a model that YIMBYs can reproduce nationally. Housing advocates have plenty more work to do in California, where much of my advocacy has been focused. Despite its fast-growing college towns, statewide permitting is flat and housing costs are rising. In too many cases, much-anticipated reforms have failed to produce much housing. But college towns have demonstrated that transforming a community requires only a small group of highly motivated people. In California and elsewhere, such groups have made the Sisyphean task of advocacy fun , hosting happy hours , run clubs , neighborhood meetups , and workshops . “It’s really easy to point to all the abstract changes that YIMBY reforms can make at some vague point in the future,” Katie Caceres, the organizing director for the Student Homes Coalition , told me. “But real friendships are what distinguish the most successful campus groups I’ve worked with.” To ensure that college towns are a prologue to a bigger housing revolution, rather than a curious exception, YIMBYs will have to follow the example these communities set by showing up to hearings, supporting candidates, organizing lobby days, suing cities, and running for office. These steps can sometimes feel fruitless in the moment, but they’re the same ones that NIMBYs took in the 1960s and ’70s to keep Berkeley so exclusive and small. These strategies worked then to suppress growth, they worked over the past decade to restart it, and they will work now to extend it across the country.
