items.originalTitle: Gift Guide for the AI Apocalypse
items.author: Illustration by Vincent Kilbride
items.title: Gift Guide for the AI Apocalypse
items.summary: A cataclysm that destroys all human life is bad for many reasons, among them the resulting uselessness of a gift guide. Setting aside an extinction scenario , the more interesting—and more likely—outcome of an AI apocalypse is one in which ordinary life continues, but changed. This is closer to the biblical sense of the term apocalypse , which means a pulling back of the curtain on a divine truth. And of all the ways to prepare for an apocalypse brought about by artificial intelligence, surely the most American would be to go shopping. Before we start, here are the rules of this AI-apocalypse shopping spree. First, the calamitous scenarios (and the giftable baubles!) must be specifically connected to artificial intelligence. A backup generator and a supply of nonperishable foods would be useful in all sorts of situations: natural disasters, conventional warfare, climatological stress, terrorism. But owning them makes you a prepper of a more generic stripe. You can find lots of gift guides of those sorts in other types of publications. Godspeed. Second, the gifts need not attempt to prevent an apocalyptic outcome from arising—as if that would even be possible—nor solve a calamity once it does. The wares we seek will not avert AI ruination, but they should help curtail its impacts in a meaningful way. Perhaps more important, pondering the gift ought to help elucidate the threat itself—and reframe our understanding of what counts as an AI calamity in the first place. [ Read: Prepare for the AI apocalypse like you’d prepare for a snowstorm ] And finally, a good AI-apocalypse gift ought to be handy now, in advance of civilization-scale doomsday. The forces that might lead to bad outcomes live in the present as much as the future. Gifts for the Loss of Shared Reality The internet has undermined truth for decades now. Blogs and social-media platforms offered an alternative to the gatekeeping of traditional media. They democratized expression but also fragmented communities. Eventually, everyone’s ability to say anything all the time helped erode the institutional authority of science and the government. Accuracy became less important than engagement. These incentives industrialized misinformation, making fabrication profitable. Personalized feeds mated to algorithmic recommendations accelerated the culture of conspiracy theories. AI threatens to eradicate the fragments of truth that remain. Misinformation used to spread by accident, simply because billions of people could say anything online. Then disinformation duped people on purpose. But AI has installed automated and personalized synthetic text, images, video, and audio absolutely everywhere. It’s overwhelming. Humankind risks suffocating in so much seemingly real but actually fake information that the distinction between the two might become erased. Reality can’t be brought back entirely, but some tools can help. The Leica M-11P is a digital camera that includes hardware-authenticated digital signatures to verify the images it creates, including a record of their provenance and changes that have been made to them. The device is somewhat bulky and extremely expensive. A related alternative: any film camera. A physical negative offers material evidence of what the camera saw. Reality Defender is a software service that uses a variety of methods to detect AI manipulation in images, audio, and video. The service is intended for corporate and industrial use at a cost of about $400 a year for 1,000 scans a month, but a free plan offers 50 image analyses each month. A print-newspaper subscription is a fixed, physical version of the daily or weekly news that allows you to hold the same information as your friends and neighbors. It also offers a record of what was reported at a given time, unperturbed by questionable summaries, screenshots, or social-media posts. Gifts for the Collapse of Expertise Artificial intelligence offers an effective solution to almost any intellectual or practical problem. It can compose an email, write a job application, tell you what to eat for dinner, build a stock portfolio, offer instructions for servicing a septic tank. Or, better put, AI can appear to offer such solutions, cheaply and instantaneously. As more people and organizations take AI outputs as presumed expertise, the people who possess actual expertise in any subject could become displaced. People may stop learning how to do things for themselves—or they may come to trust the confidence of a machine, delivered effortlessly, more than they trust other people. Unlike reality, expertise really is something you can purchase, by hiring people with knowledge, experience, and credentials to carry out tasks or offer advice. This might be a graphic designer, a structural engineer, a turf-lawn-management expert, an accountant, or a tutor in a specialized subject. Your situation, and that of the individual who might receive your gift, will be particular. The trick, of course, is finding an actual expert amid the din of faux competence. If you can, recommend people you know or have worked with personally, but if you can’t, Bark offers a directory of professionals in many domains. Wikipedia isn’t a perfect host of reliable expertise, but it’s human-made and better than many alternatives. Kiwix offers an offline version of the complete English Wikipedia—along with emergency planning, repair guides, medical references, and other resources. It’s $350 as a hardware device or $35 for the data alone. The offline version is meant to defend against infrastructural collapse, but your gift recipient could use it just to access knowledge in a deliberate, internet-disconnected way. Your local library also offers an easy way to find expertise offline. Many local libraries also give you the ability to borrow ebooks, audiobooks, and magazines via the Libby app. Libraries are generally free for residents of the municipality they serve, but you need a library card to use them—and getting one typically requires an in-person visit. Overcoming that hurdle might be harder than people think. The gift, then: Take someone to lunch and then the library to get them signed up. Illustration by Vincent Kilbride Gifts for the Decline of Relationships Lunch or dinner is great for people you already know. What about people you don’t? In 2000, the political scientist Robert Putnam published Bowling Alone , the original screed against American solitude. The title refers to bowling leagues, which were once popular sources of community but fell out of favor. Putnam’s book has been enormously influential, but many readers treat bowling leagues as a metaphor rather than a concrete activity people can and do participate in. You can still go bowling! The United States Bowling Congress can help you find local leagues , memberships in which can cost as little as $10 a week . You don’t need a bowling ball to start, but affordable sets of ball, bag, and shoes make for something you can wrap. It is curious that human relationships have become so challenging to steward, given that technology allows us to connect with one another constantly and for free. Perhaps writing letters, making long-distance phone calls, and paying people a visit in person offered greater connectivity because they demanded a break from ordinary life. Some defamiliarization might help human connections thrive. You could, I suppose, give someone a stationery set and invite them to write letters again. But that feels retrograde. Instead, consider one of the oddball examples of telepresence that have been commercialized. The Friendship Lamp , for example, comes in a set of two glowing objects, one for you and one for someone else. When one of you touches the device, the other one lights up too. Bond Touch offers a similar idea in bracelet and necklace form. Gifts for Cultural Stagnation Being an artist of any kind has always been difficult, but generative AI could erode the market for human cultural production so much that such work becomes commercially unviable. When partnered with a consolidated industry for distribution, AI could even become the dominant source of what is currently known as human expression. And if AI were to replace a sufficient quantity of original human works, culture would enter a kind of death spiral, in which no new art can arise except as rehashings of what came before. The best way to combat the automation of human culture is to support culture itself. This can’t be done just once, but must happen over and over again, as a practice. A season pass to your local symphony, theater, or ballet offers one way to help someone develop such a relationship. So does buying real art from real artists—galleries in your area are bound to offer affordable drawings, prints, paintings, and plastic arts that can help start a collection. Many bookstores feature works by local writers too. Culture would be better if more people produced it in addition to consuming it. Digital life confused that process. It appeared to democratize creation, giving everyone the tools to make music, writing, art, and moving images—and then distribute their wares globally. Online platforms also distorted culture into a thing primarily meant to produce attention and monetization. Nothing was really ever stopping you from learning to produce (and then improve) your own cultural work, whether music, writing, painting, ceramics, or whatever else that might strike you. Buy a violin or an easel (or anything of the sort that seems right for your gift recipient), along with a local class to get them started. Illustration by Vincent Kilbride Gifts for the Unabiding Din of Machines AI chats you up constantly now. Word processors, apps, even Google searches now typically initiate a conversation with an AI agent, whether you asked for one or not. Digital-detox gifts offer one way to quell the noise: for example, a redesigned but old-school media device such as the Fosi Audio compact-disc player , a deliberately limited digital device such as the Light Phone , or the Brick smartphone lock. But those options are defensive. By contrast, an array of objects that offer simple, quiet, and unmediated attention remains available. A nice mechanical wristwatch—or even a simple, cheap Casio—can do it. So can a good kitchen tool, such as an ice-cream scoop or a potato ricer. A delightful notebook and writing implement are always good for some quiet, as is a print book of almost any type. Gifts for the Digital Panopticon Years ago, information such as your home address and voting history might have been available in public records, but they were obfuscated by the need to access them in person. Online services ended that. And then, Big Tech started collecting and sharing information about you, with or without your permission. AI extends that tendency by improving machines’ abilities to infer knowledge about individuals—including intimate facts—from the ever-enlarging supply of data (including apparently innocuous data) constantly collected by apps, services, sensors, facial-recognition cameras, transaction records, and more. The ability to carry out one’s life in modest obscurity had already become difficult. AI could do away with it entirely. [ Read: Read this website while you still can ] You can buy tools that can, to some extent, defend against digital surveillance: a Faraday bag can block incoming and outgoing signals when you put your smartphone inside it; a service such as DeleteMe finds and removes information about you online; and adversarial apparel can stymie computer-vision surveillance . But you can also reduce your digital footprint in simpler ways. An envelope of cash allows your gift recipient to spend money without creating a transaction record for data-broker discovery. A nice paper planner allows you to keep a calendar without sharing your deeds with Google. Gmail can scan all of your emails for advertising targeting, something a private email account on a service such as Proton Mail or Apple iCloud+ does not. A subscription, along with a custom domain name, would make for a privacy-forward gift. Gifts for the Swamp of Sycophancy Large language models tend to affirm what a user provides as input—“I agree”—even if that entails validating flawed views or circumventing accurate responses. Over time, AI models’ designers may reduce this sycophancy effect, but they will have to overcome a strong incentive not to do so: an agreeable and even obsequious AI creates greater engagement, use, and thereby value for the AI companies. Should AI’s tendency to grovel increase while human reliance on it also expands, then a plurality of people may come to expect and acclimate to sycophancy in every nook and cranny of ordinary life. To help someone wade out of the swamp, a gift needs to offer psychological and social effects rather than utility or even delight. A demanding book of puzzles is an option, such as Cain’s Jawbone (a legendary 1934 literary puzzle) and The New York Times Seriously Hard Crossword Puzzles . A difficult or complex board game ( Car Wars , perhaps, or High Frontier 4 All ) or video game (such as Dark Souls ) could fit the bill too. Physical activity also has a role to play: A couple of trips to an indoor-climbing wall or a few consultations with a personal trainer might be enough to reveal that the world was not built for you alone. Gifts for Trust’s Twilight The loss of shared reality, fueled by the swamp of sycophancy, could cause members of the public to withdraw into their own addled, private realities. Just as likely, it could ignite paranoia. Every email, text message, phone call, viral video, and internet post that seems authentic might also be fake. AI impersonation, already enormously convincing, is poised to improve, and tools to detect evidence of AI intervention in text and audiovisual material remain dubious. Once every shard of apparently earnest or human-created content raises suspicion, almost nothing will seem trustworthy. When trust itself cannot be assumed, perhaps ever, an almost delusional suspicion may become the default mode of interaction. Some companies are trying to solve the trust problems that computers create with … more computers. Hardware-security keys such as YubiKey offer better protection against phishing and hacking attacks than password managers or two-factor authentication. And Vicem, designed to avert telephone scams, offers an AI phone monitor . Other, simpler tools also exist. You can still get a landline number that you don’t share publicly—or a supposedly private virtual number from a service such as GetUnlisted . A more baroque (and affected) solution from the past: a personalized wax seal , along with stationery on which to apply it. Illustration by Vincent Kilbride Gifts for the End of Serendipity Optimization and efficiency, once values of business alone, have leaked into ordinary life. The practice of living one’s life—dating, parenting, dining out, working, even seeking leisure—has turned into accomplishing tasks along the way to supposedly even better tasks. In the end, human life may turn away from any encounter whose outcome is not predictable, even known in advance. Contingency, accident, and improvisation could disappear as people eschew those putatively useless disomforts—and then forget about them entirely. In a way, a good gift of any kind—AI-aware or not—counts as a gift of serendipity. Something given as a true surprise, and perhaps even absent of need, offers a door to an unexpected act. I can’t tell you what might count as such a gift for the individuals on your list; consider it a gift of judgment to ponder the matter. One idea: a paper map or atlas, the kind that can live in a car’s seat-back pocket. It might inspire someone to use a city absent computer guidance. Serendipity may be on the decline, but many of the sources that once delivered it remain available, if in fragile forms. A monthly print-magazine subscription ( such as this one ) puts a package of surprising stories in the mailbox on the regular. A short-wave radio , or an HDTV antenna and HDHomeRun device, delivers whatever is being broadcast right now to your home. A gift certificate to a local shop with no online ordering, or to a local restaurant that does not offer delivery, can ignite the delight of browsing again. A n apocalypse feels like something you can do nothing about beyond panicking or hunkering down, as if awaiting a meteor’s collision with Earth. [ Read: What if the apocalypse is already here? ] But “apocalypse” may not be the right way to understand the distinctive challenges that artificial intelligence presents to human life. The temptation to catastrophize—an urge the internet rewarded long before AI—can obscure the ways that ordinary life can steer nimbly around cataclysm simply by each of us making modest choices where alternatives are available. When carried out in the best spirit, gifts allow recipients and givers alike to see the world, and their place in it, in a marginally different light. This makes the holidays an ideal time to imagine and then embrace slightly different ways of living. None of artificial intelligence’s apocalypses, at least the ones humankind might survive, represents wholly new circumstances that AI invented. Instead, artificial intelligence wore deeper ruts into prior habits. One such rut is the discourse surrounding artificial intelligence: Either the world will be saved by AI, or else AI will ruin it. You and I and all of the people on your holiday gift list get cast as passengers, careening toward deliverance or doom. The reality will probably be more banal. Most of AI’s threats are not existential, and likewise many of the defenses against those threats will not defeat the technology. The survival equipment suitable to fortify against that erosion will be correspondingly ordinary. A notebook preserves the capacity to write. A violin hands down the experience of making music. A dinner out demands face-to-face interactions with friends. A telephone whose number only a few people know rings with delight rather than foreboding. A paper map requires interpretation; a library invites perusal; a bowling lane can facilitate new conversation. The world is not ending.

items.originalTitle: Wisconsin prisoner looks toward freedom after historic commutation
items.author: Natalie Yahr / Wisconsin Watch
items.title: Wisconsin prisoner looks toward freedom after historic commutation
items.summary: Reading Time: 5 minutes Sammy Cole still thinks about the day, 25 years ago, when he walked up to a car at a drive-up ATM in Calumet County and pointed a gun at the two young women inside. One of the women was so scared, he remembers, that she couldn’t get her card into the machine. He settled for the $80 in her wallet. A judge sentenced him to 35 years in prison, plus another 10 years of extended supervision. His release date was set for 2036. Now, following a historic announcement from the governor’s office, the 53-year-old is preparing to go home much sooner. On Nov. 13, Gov. Tony Evers shortened the sentences of 14 Wisconsin prisoners , including Cole. It’s the first time a Wisconsin governor has issued commutations since 1995 . Hundreds of Wisconsinites applied for commutations in the months after Evers reopened the process in April. Cole was one of the first applicants selected to make his case. The revival of commutations has sparked praise from prisoner advocates and criticism from judges , district attorneys and Republican lawmakers. At the inaugural meeting of the Commutations Advisory Board in August, Cole said he felt “profound regret and shame” about his crime. “At the time, I was under the complete grip of a severe addiction, and I made a terrible choice … I caused these two women to face the fear of harm to satisfy my addiction to heroin, and I’m fully aware that I caused their family torment.” Cole told the board that he’d apologized for his actions at his sentencing hearing, “but that apology was worthless without some action.” While in prison, Cole earned a high school equivalency diploma and certificates in custodial services, entrepreneurship, human relations and fork lift operating. He’s assisted elderly and disabled prisoners, mentored youth, trained service dogs and worked in the kitchen, according to the governor’s office. “I spent my years in prison doing all I can to be a better person from the very beginning of my incarceration,” Cole said. “I didn’t waste no time.” Evers commuted Cole’s sentence to 28 years in prison and 10 under extended supervision “in recognition of his positive adjustments and rehabilitation while incarcerated.” A few days after the news broke, Wisconsin Watch spoke to Cole about his plans. While the announcement said Cole would spend another four years in prison, Cole said he might get out in just a few months if he can get a slot in the state’s Earned Release Program, a treatment program through which some people with a history of substance use disorder can qualify for early release with less than four years remaining on their sentences. The popular program is notoriously backlogged : As of September, more than 2,200 people were on the waiting list. Cole is still waiting to hear whether he will remain eligible following his commutation. “It’s just more rehabilitation … so when I get out there, I have even more tools and resources to help me with my success when I re-enter society,” he said. The following interview has been edited for length and clarity. How did you hear that your sentence had been commuted? I got the news from other inmates. They happened to see the news. I was in the room at the time reading, and I didn’t have a clue what was going on. A lot of guys knocked on my door and told me that I had gained a commutation. Then I started receiving messages from family, and then I found out it had been commuted to 28 years. I was immediately really happy and excited. It was a huge relief that all my years of hard work to rehabilitate myself and develop a positive, productive lifestyle paid off — that it was recognized and understood that I could be a member of society again. I did all this to better myself. I had no clue that one day the governor would decide to make an executive order to give a guy a chance to gain his freedom. It was a beautiful thing. It also has been heartbreaking for a lot of other guys, guys that I’ve been incarcerated with for 20-plus years that are equally as deserving to gain their freedom. We’re like a big support group helping each other get through this process. What was the hardest thing about applying for commutation? The hardest thing was that I had to put myself out there again and burden my family again with this hope that maybe I could come home. So it was like, “Should I do this? This might just be some political ploy. Is the governor really going to do this?” That was probably the main thing: I didn’t want to disappoint my family again. Do you know yet whether you’re still eligible for Earned Release? The social worker on our unit says she’s waiting for official information from our records department, and so no one knows anything. I (was eligible for) the Earned Release Program already as it stood, but the Department of Corrections controls placement. They only let you in these programs when you’re like six to 18 months from your release date, which is a disastrous policy. A guy like me who’s been incarcerated 25 years — if it wasn’t for my drive to better myself, then I would have been sitting around doing nothing, playing cards or dominoes or participating in negative activities. A lot of guys do that, and as a result, when it comes time for them to get ready to go home, (the Department of Corrections is) cramming programs into them, and (the prisoners) are just going through the formalities. The sincerity is not there. I think it’s important to begin your rehabilitation as soon as you come through Assessment and Evaluation at Dodge Correctional Institution. I think the Department of Corrections should begin instilling in inmates their rehabilitative mode so that they can start changing their life around early in their incarceration. If they did, the turnover would be a lot better. Guys like me and older guys are trying to help these young guys. A lot of guys don’t want to work a (prison) job. They feel like, “I’m paying restitution and (they’re) taking 60% of my money,” but it’s not about the money. It’s about acquiring work skills for when you get out in society. A lot of these guys were drug dealers or had drug issues. They need to acquire new skills, a whole new lifestyle. For the commutations process, applicants have to explain what their plans are when they get out. What was it like for you to try to figure out where you’d live or where you’d work? A few years ago, I completed Defy Ventures ’ entrepreneurs-in-training program (through UW-Madison Extension). They help you to get a job when you gain your freedom. They give you a mentor, and they are by your side for the first year. In addition, I have a grandmother that died some years ago that left her house to us grandkids in Chicago. She thought that I was going to be getting out of prison in 2016 when I became eligible for the Earned Release Program. Granddad had died some years before that from Alzheimer’s, and she wanted me to be there to be by her side, and I couldn’t be there. Right now, (my cousin and siblings) are getting the house all fixed up for me so I have a residence to go to. Do you know what kind of work you might do when you get out? I have a cousin in Chicago who does some advocacy things, and my brother is active in Chicago as a mentor for kids trying to get out of gangs. I’ve got skills as a forklift operator and I’m also a journeyman in custodial services. And I’m interested to see if I could get a job where my granddaddy worked at (Illinois aerospace and defense manufacturer Northrop Grumman). He was actually a high-paid janitor for a number of years, so I might show up there and fill out an application and see, as a descendant of my granddad, could I gain a job there? So I don’t think I’m going to have any problems with gaining employment at all. Natalie Yahr reports on pathways to success statewide for Wisconsin Watch, working in partnership with Open Campus . Email her at nyahr@wisconsinwatch.org . items.author: Katie Hawthorne
items.title: Pummelling electronic trio Factory Floor’s first album in a decade shows signs of mellowing – but is it all a feint?
items.summary: (Phantasy Sound) One of the buzziest acts of the 2010s return with One Trip, which bathes their classic sound in a warmer light – until the buzzsaw synths and scattershot percussion explode Devotees still speak in hushed awe about the intense, hypnotic performances by Factory Floor, one of the buzziest electronic groups of the 2010s. Even the band agree: Nik Colk Void (vocalist and modular synth wrangler) wistfully remembered them as “full of carnage” during their lengthy hiatus. So what on earth went down at Mutek Montreal in 2024? Their one-off reunion show proved so transformative that it inspired Factory Floor’s first album in 10 years. Sounding uncharacteristically relaxed, opening single Continuation is a woozier take on their often grinding approach to repetition, building into blissful contentment rather than rabid euphoria. “It’s gonna be fun,” Void exhales. “It’s gonna be … easy.” This third album takes in Factory Floor’s favoured influences – brain-spinning industrial noise, eccentric acid techno, a Kraftwerkian clarity of purpose – and bathes them in a warmer light. But that’s not to say they’ve softened. Standout track Buzz Saw has the album’s toughest synth line, serrated and stomping, for what should be a new live classic.

items.originalTitle: Affidavit ballot scramble increase calls for Mississippi early voting
items.author: Taylor Vance
items.title: Affidavit ballot scramble increase calls for Mississippi early voting
items.summary: As voters across Mississippi arrived at the polls on Election Day only to find their names missing from the poll books, they were forced to cast affidavit ballots, leaving them frustrated and wondering whether their vote would count. Mississippi is one of three states without early voting, which funnels most voting into a single day. Advocates say that magnified the chaos this year and forced many voters to cast a affidavit ballots, and delayed final results of the midterm Senate election. Candidates, advocates and voters now say Mississippi should join the overwhelming majority of states by allowing some form of early voting to reduce the number of affidavit ballots cast during an election and correct some mistakes ahead of time. “We have been singing this song for as long as I can recall, but definitely if we had early voting, that would be helpful and truly we wouldn’t have as much of the chaos,” Democratic Rep. Timaka James-Jones of Belzoni said. James-Jones, a former county circuit clerk, said early voting would reduce the number of affidavit ballots and she believes voters who cast affidavit ballots are likely to be in the same position next time because the underlying problem never gets corrected. Instead of early voting, Mississippi has absentee voting. To vote absentee, a voter must list one of about 10 legal excuses for not casting an in-person vote on Election Day. For example, a voter can cast an absentee ballot if they plan to be out of town on Election Day or if they are a college student. One of the major opponents of early voting is Republican Gov. Tate Reeves. On Election Day, he wrote on social media that he and First Lady Elee Reeves voted “IN-PERSON. On Election Day. With a Valid Photo ID. Just like every other person in America should be required to do.” His opposition has been decisive before. Senate leaders ended the 2025 session without sending Reeves a bill that would have expanded pre-Election Day voting, and he would likely have vetoed it. He had called no-excuse early voting bad for election integrity after the Senate passed that bill. But it appears even his own party is leaving him behind. The Mississippi Republican Party sent a mailer out before the election encouraging voters in large print to “vote early” for GOP candidates. In smaller letters toward the bottom, it said “vote absentee before October 31 or head to the polls on Election Day, November 3.” President Donald Trump before the election also said on social media that in-person early voting was “UNDERWAY NOW” in Mississippi, which was inaccurate. Senate Elections Chairman Jeremy England, a Republican from Vancleave, has pushed early voting legislation through the Legislature for years, but it’s failed to advance out of the Capitol. He has said constituents are frustrated and confused to learn Mississippi has no early voting. Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson is responsible for administering parts of the state’s elections and provides training to county election officials. He recently told reporters that he is “an old school guy who loves Election Day” voting at the precinct but doesn’t oppose early voting laws. He argued that in-person absentee voting already functions as a form of early voting Wakinya Clanton, the state director of the Southern Poverty Law Center, also supports early voting, but she said the state’s vote-counting system needs a complete overhaul, including same-day voter registration. “We need early voting without stipulations,” she said. “You don’t need an excuse to vote. If you’re a Mississippian, you should be able to participate in the election.” The Mississippi Legislature will convene on Jan. 5 for its regular session.

items.summary: Published nearly two years after his death, this edited selection of the Argentinian pope’s diary capture the profundity of his faith – just don’t expect revelations or raciness When the cardinals in Rome elected the Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio as the 266th pope of the Roman Catholic church in March 2013 – the first Latin American, the first pontiff born outside Europe since the 8th century, the first Jesuit and the first to take the name Francis (after Saint Francis of Assisi) – many of us lapsed Catholics gave a small cheer. Here was a man who looked fair to change the increasingly fusty and conservative, authoritarian and admonitory, tendencies of his two predecessors. Bergoglio seemingly did not want the ceremonial trappings of the office – he’d bought himself a return ticket home to Buenos Aires and caught the bus back to the Vatican guest house where the other cardinals were staying, insisting he would not be moving into the papal apartments overlooking St Peter’s Square.
